name: Context
blurb: FLEX inside GOV.UK Once: the people it serves, its sibling systems, and the one organisation outside the boundary its request handling exchanges data with. C4 level 1 — runtime only.
audience: Anyone new to FLEX, including non-engineers
note: 6 domains · 3 service gateways · 2 shared APIs · 277+ AWS resources in production

d.role: The GOV.UK Once programme. FLEX, the GOV.UK App, the Cognito user pool, UDP and UNS all sit inside it; DVLA and GOV.UK One Login do not.
facts: A sibling system here is one FLEX reaches by assuming a role named in its consumer-config secret and dialling a private endpoint — not one it shares infrastructure with.
Only one line leaves this box carrying FLEX traffic: FLEX to DVLA. The Cognito to One Login federation also crosses it, but FLEX is not on that hop.

d.role: Uses the GOV.UK App. Never contacts FLEX directly.
facts: Reaches FLEX only through the app, carrying a Cognito access token.
Identified downstream by a single pairwise ID — the token's username claim.

The authorizer passes only the pairwise ID; the one exception is udp's POST /v1/identity/:service, which is handed the raw Authorization header and reads the token's sub claim to verify the DVLA session hash.

d.role: The only external production caller of the public API; FLEX's own smoke-test Lambda also calls /app/udp/v1/users/me every five minutes.
facts: Calls /app/{domain}/{version}/… over HTTPS with a Bearer token.
Signs the user in through Cognito's hosted UI, which federates to GOV.UK One Login; FLEX is not in the loop and only ever sees the resulting Cognito access token.

d.role: Exposes GOV.UK Once domain APIs to the app, and brokers every call those domains make to a sibling system or a third party.
facts: One shared public API for the app, one shared private API for everything internal.
Six domains and three service gateways, all generated from declarative config; three of the six domains list production in their environments.
A domain never holds a credential for anything upstream — only the service gateways do.
The FLEX team owns all of this infrastructure, and today owns the domain code too — CODEOWNERS carries a TODO to hand /domains/{name} to each domain team as it onboards.
Stores no user state and has no asynchronous path: no database, no queue, no event bus. UDP, UNS and DVLA are the systems of record, so every request is a synchronous fan-out.

d.role: Issues the access tokens FLEX verifies on every public request, and runs the hosted sign-in UI the app uses.
facts: Provisioned outside FLEX; the pool and client IDs arrive as configuration through flex-params.
FLEX asserts issuer, token_use=access and client ID, then takes the username claim as the pairwise ID.
In development a stub JWKS Function URL stands in, so tests can self-sign tokens.

d.tech: OIDC identity provider federated into the Cognito user pool
d.role: Authenticates the user. Cognito federates to it; FLEX never calls it and never sees a One Login token.
facts: Run by GDS, so it sits outside the GOV.UK Once programme but inside government — DVLA is still the only separate organisation on this diagram.

The hosted-UI authorize call carries idpidentifier=onelogin; the sign-in host comes from the auth/one-login-environment parameter — signin.account.gov.uk in production, signin.{env}.account.gov.uk elsewhere.
No FLEX runtime code drives this flow. The only copy of it in this repo is the token generator the E2E tests and the smoke-test canary use.

d.tech: AWS API behind a private endpoint · SigV4
d.role: System of record for identity links, user records, notification preferences and group subscriptions.
facts: The hub of the domain graph: dvla (via the udp domain), groups and example all reach it. uns only calls FLEX's own udp domain for a locally-derived push ID.
Notification, group and identity-exchange requests carry a requesting-service: app header; the remaining routes authenticate with the API key alone.
local-council also declares udp-gateway integrations, to /v1/local-council/*, but the udp gateway defines no such routes — those calls fail at runtime today.

d.tech: AWS API behind a private endpoint · SigV4
d.role: System of record for notification records and group subscriptions.
facts: Its consumer config carries both an apiUrl and a privateApiUrl; the gateway client is built on privateApiUrl, so FLEX never uses a public route to reach it.
Every uns domain route first derives the user's push ID from the pairwise ID via FLEX's udp domain, then calls UNS with it — the derivation is an in-FLEX HMAC, not a UDP call.

d.role: Driving licence, customer vehicle, share code and vehicle enquiry services, run by a separate agency.
facts: DVLA models GOV.UK as an external consumer: the authenticate call is literally /thirdparty-access/v1/authenticate.
Reached over the internet through a NAT gateway rather than a private endpoint — the same egress path the authorizer uses to fetch the Cognito JWKS, since there is no cognito-idp VPC endpoint.
Fronted inside FLEX by the dvla domain and the dvla service gateway — those are FLEX components, not this system.
The user is never a direct FLEX client.

d.protocol: HTTPS · OAuth 2.0 authorization code with PKCE against the hosted UI
d.auth: The user's own credentials, checked by One Login
d.carries: An authorization code, exchanged for a Cognito access token
facts: The one edge here that legitimately bypasses FLEX — FLEX sees none of it, only the token that comes out.

d.protocol: HTTPS · OIDC redirect from the Cognito hosted UI
d.carries: The sign-in itself — email, password and the authenticator code
facts: The code comes back to the app's govuk://govuk/login-auth-callback redirect URI and is exchanged at Cognito's /oauth2/token, so what the app ends up holding is a Cognito token, not a One Login one.

d.auth: Cognito access token in the Authorization header
facts: Structurally checked by a CloudFront Function at the edge — segment count, JSON, no alg:none, signature present — then cryptographically verified by the Lambda authorizer.

d.auth: None — the JWKS document is public
facts: Issuer, token_use and client ID are all asserted, not just the signature.
The verifier is built inside the handler, so the environment is re-parsed on every invocation.

d.protocol: HTTPS via the API Gateway interface endpoint
d.auth: sts:AssumeRole then SigV4, plus an x-api-key header
d.carries: Identity links, users, notification preferences, groups
facts: The assumed-role credential provider is held in a module-level map, so warm containers reuse the one-hour STS credential and only refresh it in its last five minutes.
Never leaves the VPC.

d.protocol: HTTPS via the API Gateway interface endpoint
d.auth: sts:AssumeRole then SigV4, plus an X-API-KEY header
facts: The API key is set once on the client, so it rides on every UNS call rather than being chosen per route.
Never leaves the VPC.

d.protocol: HTTPS through a NAT gateway, on an unsigned client
d.auth: X-API-KEY plus a DVLA-issued bearer token from a username and password authenticate call
d.carries: Licence, vehicle, share-code and vehicle-enquiry operations
facts: The one line in this diagram that crosses the GOV.UK Once boundary.
Only the DVLA service gateway holds the username, password and API key; the calling domain handles nothing but the session token they produce.
